title: Decode the composition task
summary: Identify the topic, command, audience, scope and required personal application before planning a composition.

sections.title: Answer the task that was set
content: A fluent composition can still lose relevance if it answers a nearby question instead of the actual task. Before generating ideas, separate what the prompt requires from ideas that merely seem related.
Read the entire prompt once without planning. On the second read, mark five features: topic, command, audience, scope and personal application. These features become the boundaries of the response.

sections.title: Use the T-C-A-S-P check
content: Topic names the subject you must discuss. Command states the thinking job, such as explain, describe, argue or reflect. Audience identifies the intended reader and therefore affects tone, detail and vocabulary.

Scope limits the response: how many ideas, which setting, what time frame, what text form and which examples belong. Personal application tells you whether the task requires your own experience, a realistic future use or a personal judgment.
Turn each feature into a short note. If the prompt does not name an audience, write ‘general exam reader’ and use clear, controlled English rather than inventing a specialised reader.

sections.title: Decode one original prompt
content: Practice prompt: ‘The ASEAN Youth Learning Blog asks students to share practical lessons. Write an article for secondary-school readers about one skill or idea you learned at school. Explain how you have used it, or could use it, in a different area of your life. Support your response with a specific example.’

Topic: one school-learned skill or idea. Command: explain its use beyond the original lesson. Audience: secondary-school readers of a youth blog. Scope: one skill or idea, one different area of life, and at least one specific example. Personal application: an actual use or a realistic use you could make.
A response about why education matters generally would be related but off-task. A response listing three school subjects would also break the one-focus scope.

sections.title: Separate requirements from possibilities
content: Label exact requirements R. Label useful choices C. In the practice prompt, writing for secondary-school readers and giving a specific example are requirements. Choosing teamwork, budgeting or scientific observation is a choice.

Do not turn a choice into a false requirement. The prompt does not require a dramatic success, a particular school subject or a completely true past event because ‘could use’ permits a realistic future application.

sections.title: Write a one-sentence task contract
content: Combine the five notes into one task contract before planning: ‘I will explain to secondary-school readers how one school-learned skill applies in another area of life, using one specific actual or realistic example.’
Check every proposed paragraph against this contract. If a paragraph neither explains the application nor supports the example, revise or remove it.

sections.title: Diagnose prompt-reading errors
content: Topic drift means the response moves to a broad related theme. Command loss means it narrates or lists when the prompt asks for explanation. Audience mismatch means the tone or assumed knowledge does not suit the named reader.

Scope breach means the response ignores a limit such as one idea or a specific setting. Missing personal link means it discusses a concept without showing an actual or realistic use in the writer’s life.

sections.title: Decode before you plan
content: Analyse the original practice prompt in six steps. Complete the whole group before viewing feedback, then compare your choices with the task contract.
